🚀 Gala Swap isn't just another DEX. It’s a powerful engine built to capture value directly from market inefficiencies, and it’s fueling a serious opportunity for liquidity providers.

Here’s the breakdown on why this is a potential game-changer, especially for new pools:

The Arbitrage Engine Is Already Running

Let's talk about that brand-new pool you just saw launch. How does it earn anything on day one? The answer is simple: Arbitrage.

The moment a pool goes live, its price can slightly differ from the prices on major centralized exchanges (CEX). Smart traders and automated bots, known as arbitrageurs, are constantly scanning for these tiny gaps. They buy where it’s cheap and sell where it’s dear.

This isn't theoretical volume. Even today, with only a handful of live pools on Gala Swap, millions of dollars in arbitrage volume are flowing through the platform daily. Every single one of those trades pays a fee to the liquidity provider (LP).

Real Volume, Real Fees (Not "Farm Token" Emissions)

This is what makes Gala Swap different. The yield isn't based on inflationary "farm token" emissions that you have to constantly race against.

The LP rewards on Gala Swap are generated by real trading activity—the essential work of keeping the DEX price in sync with the broader market. When you provide liquidity, you become the infrastructure that makes this flow possible, and you earn your share of the fees from that volume.

The Real Gold Rush: Expanding the Surface

The current volume is impressive, but here’s what’s truly exciting: the bottleneck isn't the demand from traders; it's the surface area available for the arbitrage engine to work across.

A few dozen pools can only capture a few dozen tokens' worth of flow. Imagine this same efficient arbitrage engine running across hundreds of pools that simply don't exist yet.

The Takeaway:

The traders are ready. The volume is real. The arbitrage engine is already running. What's missing is the liquidity to serve that volume and capture those fees across a much broader range of pairs.

Gala Swap provides the infrastructure; you provide the liquidity to unlock the full potential. 🟡

Last night was a tremendous blessing here in Tauranga - though not without its challenges.

It began with my flight from Auckland, which was delayed and on the brink of cancellation due to thick fog. Then, as we gathered at Shoreline Calvary, a group of 30-35 loud and aggressive pro-Palestinian protesters attempted to disrupt both services. They banged on the windows, poured fake “blood” across the entrance, and used loud sound and flashing lights in an effort to silence me and intimidate the church staff and attendees. As they screamed, “Free Palestine!” and “From the river to the sea!” they once again revealed the same demonic spirit that openly calls for the destruction of the Jewish state.

But God…

Pastor Doug, his wonderful wife Destiny, and their phenomenal team at Shoreline Calvary stood firm. We had two consecutive full-house services filled with heartfelt worship, sweet fellowship, and a deep study of God’s Word. What the enemy intended for intimidation, God turned into encouragement and blessing.

I thank the Lord for yet another fruitful stop here in New Zealand.

Today we travel to Hamilton for a sweet gathering with the Calvary Chapel family. I am fully convinced that He who began this good work will be faithful to continue blessing this tour tonight and in the days ahead.

Meanwhile, in the Middle East, Israel is bracing for another round of confrontation with Iran.

It looks like my journey back home may be yet another adventure…

But God!

Thank you all for your fervent prayers and faithful support!

Onwards and upwards!

Awaiting His Return,

Amir Tsarfati

🔥 Night 12: Hormuz as Reality Show

On the twelfth straight night, CENTCOM pressed “repeat.” At 5:30 p.m. Eastern, another wave of US strikes rolled over Iran’s coast, sold with the same copy‑paste line as every night before: protecting “civilian mariners and commercial vessels” in regional shipping lanes. 

By morning, the target list read like a demolition tour — naval assets, missile and drone storage, coastal surveillance sites, air defenses — wrapped in a promo slogan about “more than 50,000 American service members” staying “alert, focused, lethal and most ready” across the Middle East.

The map of hits filled in overnight: Bandar Abbas, Ramshir in Khuzestan, Bushehr, Sirik port, Kharg, Ahvaz, the islands of Kishm and Qeshm, Tabriz, Zanjan, Kermanshah province for the first time since Operation Roaring Lion, Jask, Konarak and Mahshahr. 

Khuzestan’s deputy governor reported missile strikes near Ahvaz; Bushehr’s governor confirmed attacks in the city and said a power station was hit by a US missile near the nuclear plant, a detail echoed by Arab media. 

Local agencies added another wave on a military site. At the Shalamcheh crossing, likely aimed at an Iranian border‑guard HQ, officials admitted two deaths. 

Opposition channels spoke of more, naming one victim as Amir Mohammad Salami of the Revolutionary Guards’ signals corps and noting that Iran’s national police chief, Ahmad‑Reza Radan, had visited the crossing hours before the strike.

For the first time since fighting resumed 12 days ago, long‑range B‑1B bombers from British bases were used against IRGC targets — even as US briefers insisted that bombers weren’t flown “last night,” and official footage from the south showed little more than a pier, a shovel and a boat. 

On the other side of the water, reports from Jask spoke of wounded and strikes on IRGC navy bases; state TV literally asked civilians to shoot down enemy drones and helicopters themselves. 

The Guards announced that no tanker would pass Hormuz without their coordination, claimed two tankers had turned back and one had caught fire, and later there were reports of explosions on Kishm island and in the strait, plus a missile hitting its shore. 

Meanwhile, IRGC units handed out shoulder‑launched Misagh heat‑seeking missiles — Chinese‑based SK‑7s with a range of up to six kilometers — to Basij activists and junior personnel. The army that runs advanced air‑defense batteries is now asking its citizens to point second‑hand launchers at the sky and hope.

So the twelfth night looks like this. The world’s biggest navy carpet‑bombs “maritime threats” with strategic bombers. 

The regime that closed Hormuz orders villagers to shoot drones with export knock‑offs. 

Between them, 2,000 ships and tens of thousands of sailors sit stuck on both sides of a strait that used to be an energy corridor and is now a live‑fire exhibition. 

Security is the word both sides use. Hostage is the reality everyone else lives.
